summary: Describes source-specific multicast for IP. IPv4 addresses in 232/8 and IPv6 addresses with the FF3x::/32 prefix are reserved for SSM, where receivers ask for traffic from a particular source to a group address. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: With ordinary multicast you hear anyone speaking in a room. With SSM you pick the speaker, and set aside special addresses for it.

subtitle: Multicast where a receiver names the exact sender it wants, using reserved address ranges.

tldr.problem: Classic IP multicast delivers a group's traffic from any sender to anyone who joins, which needs extra router machinery and lets two senders on the same group address interfere.
tldr.mechanism: IPv4 addresses 232/8 and IPv6 addresses FF3x::/32 are set aside for source-specific multicast. A receiver subscribes to a channel, a source address S plus a group address G, and routers forward only that traffic.
tldr.outcome: Hosts and routers that support SSM must follow the rules in this RFC, including IGMPv3 or MLDv2 on hosts and the PIM-SSM subset of PIM-SM on routers. It is a Proposed Standard and nothing obsoletes it.

today: RFC 4607 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2006. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The multicast model in RFC 1112 delivers a datagram sent to a multicast address G to every upper-layer module that asked for G. This document calls that model Any-Source Multicast (ASM). It supports both one-to-many and many-to-many communication.

RFC 4607 defines Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), an extension to the Internet network service for datagrams sent to a reserved range of addresses. It lists three benefits: no cross-delivery when two sources use the same destination address, no need for hosts to coordinate address choice, and no need for many of the router protocols that ASM requires. For example, the shared trees and Rendezvous Points of PIM-SM are not needed.

Like ASM, an SSM sender is not told who or how many the receivers are. SSM suits dissemination-style applications whose senders are known before the application starts. It does not directly support multicast resource discovery, where a client sends a query to a service location group.
sections.eli5: Normal multicast is like a loudspeaker anyone can talk into. SSM is like tuning to one named radio station, so nobody else's noise gets mixed in.

sections.title: Channels and SSM Semantics
sections.content:
The service is defined simply. A datagram with source address S and an SSM destination address G is delivered to each host socket that has specifically asked for datagrams sent by S to G, and only to those sockets. The pair (S,G) is called a channel. Any host may send to an SSM address.

Because the source is part of the channel's identity, many senders can reuse the same G without conflict. For example, (192.0.2.1, 232.7.8.9) and (192.0.2.2, 232.7.8.9) are different channels, and so are the IPv6 pairs (2001:3618::1, FF33::1234) and (2001:3618::2, FF33::1234).

It is meaningless to ask for traffic to an SSM address G without naming a source, and routers MUST ignore such a request.
sections.eli5: A channel is a TV channel plus the name of the station sending it. Two stations can use the same channel number and you still only get the one you asked for.

sections.title: Terminology: Groups Versus Channels
sections.content:
To avoid confusion the RFC uses separate words for the two models. Ordinary ASM addresses identify a host group by a single address G, and receivers use Join(G) and Leave(G). SSM addresses identify a channel by (S,G), and receivers use Subscribe(S,G) and Unsubscribe(S,G).

The RFC notes that although this is a new service model for applications, the protocols needed to support it are largely a subset of those used for ASM.
sections.eli5: Joining a group is like walking into a crowded room. Subscribing to a channel is like phoning one particular friend.

sections.title: SSM Addresses and Their Allocation
sections.content:
For IPv4, the range 232/8 (232.0.0.0 to 232.255.255.255) is designated for SSM. For IPv6 the prefix is FF3x::/32, where x is any valid scope identifier. SSM addresses must have P=1, T=1 and plen=0, and the network prefix field must also be zero, so addresses are allocated within FF3x::/96. A system should still treat all of FF3x::/32 as SSM, to allow for future uses of the prefix field.

Some addresses are special. 232.0.0.0 and FF3x::4000:0000 are reserved and must not be used as destinations, so that one invalid SSM address is always available as a null value. The range 232.0.0.1 to 232.0.0.255 and FF3x::4000:0001 to FF3x::7FFF:FFFF are reserved for IANA allocation. FF3x::0000:0000 to FF3x::3FFF:FFFF are invalid, and a router or host MAY drop packets sent there.

Everything else is allocated locally by the sending host. A host MUST NOT allocate sequentially from the first allowed address, and RECOMMENDED practice is to pick randomly while avoiding duplicates and reserved addresses. The reason is that on Ethernet the link-layer multicast address ignores the source, so sequential allocation would make many channels share one link-layer address.

For IPv6, scoped SSM addresses are made by choosing a scope identifier. No globally agreed administratively scoped range exists for IPv4 SSM, so scoping there is done by filtering at domain boundary routers.
sections.eli5: A big block of phone numbers is set aside just for this. Each sender picks numbers at random from the block so two senders rarely pick the same one.

sections.title: Host and Router Requirements
sections.content:
Hosts get a new abstract interface, Subscribe(socket, source-address, group-address, interface) and a matching Unsubscribe. When the first socket on a host subscribes to a channel on an interface, the host IP module sends a request on that interface; when the last one unsubscribes, it sends an unsubscription. These are typically IGMPv3 messages for IPv4 or MLDv2 messages for IPv6, and a supporting host MUST implement the host side of both. An incoming SSM datagram MUST be delivered only to sockets whose subscription matches its source, destination and arriving interface. Because link layers like Ethernet ignore the source when choosing the link-layer address, the IP module MUST filter packets before passing them up.

A router MUST silently drop an SSM datagram unless a neighbouring host or router has asked for traffic from that source to that destination. A supporting router MUST implement the PIM-SSM subset of PIM-SM and the router side of IGMPv3 and MLDv2, and the PIM-SSM implementation MUST at least be able to use the unicast topology database to find a loop-free path for the explicit join.

A router that receives a non-source-specific (*,G) request for an SSM address, whether an IGMPv1 or IGMPv2 report or a PIM-SM (*,G) join, MUST NOT create forwarding state from it and MUST NOT propagate it. All routers must treat all IANA-allocated SSM addresses with source-specific semantics.
sections.eli5: Your computer tells the nearest router exactly which sender it wants. The router only passes along that sender's messages and throws away the rest.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IPsec AH and ESP can secure SSM traffic if receivers use a multicast-capable IPsec implementation. With older RFC 2401 IPsec, two senders that use the same destination address and the same SPI collide at a receiver subscribed to both, though the RFC says a conflict is unlikely by chance since the tuple has 56 bits that are generally randomly chosen.

A host can attempt denial of service by making many subscriptions, which creates (S,G) state and processing in routers. Routers MAY limit the subscription rate or count per interface or host, but the RFC warns that tight limits could inhibit future applications that use many channels. A router SHOULD verify that a subscription's source is valid for the receiving interface.

Source spoofing could let an attacker send on someone else's channel, so applications needing strong authentication should not assume all packets came from the requested source. Routing protocols used for SSM SHOULD include a reverse-path forwarding check, and an SSM router SHOULD by default disallow source routing to an SSM destination. Administrative scoping should not be relied on as a security measure.
sections.eli5: Someone could pretend to be your favourite sender or flood a router with requests. Routers can check where requests come from and set limits, but you should not blindly trust what arrives.

sections.title: Transition and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
A compliant host sends only source-specific reports for SSM addresses, and a router MUST ignore IGMPv1, IGMPv2 or MLDv1 reports for them. Forwarding every G packet to anyone who subscribed to any (S,G) would let SSM work through non-SSM routers, but the RFC says that burdens the network and is specifically not compliant with Section 5.2.

IANA allocates 232.0.0.1 through 232.0.0.255 and FF3x::4000:0001 to FF3x::7FFF:FFFF under IETF Consensus, for services that need a well-known SSM address. Apart from those, IANA SHALL NOT assign any SSM destination address to a particular entity or application, because that would undermine hosts picking addresses on their own from a large flat space.
sections.eli5: Old equipment must not be allowed to pretend it understands the new rules. Apart from a small reserved set, nobody owns any of the special addresses.

viz.caption: BENEFITS OF SSM LISTED IN THE RFC

items.title: No cross-delivery
items.text: Two sources using the same SSM address do not interfere.

items.title: No coordination
items.text: Hosts choose addresses without agreeing with each other first.

items.title: Simpler routers
items.text: Shared trees and Rendezvous Points are not needed.
